transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

I've started a sourced answer for you. Here is the short version.

**Report PR-AUC as your main number, and show ROC-AUC next to it if your manager expects to see it.**

**Why:**
- **ROC-AUC can look good when the model is only so-so.** It measures how well the model ranks churners above non-churners, and non-churners are 97% of your data. A model can flag a lot of non-churners by mistake and still score a high ROC-AUC, because those mistakes are small next to the huge number of true negatives.
- **PR-AUC follows what your manager cares about.** It tracks precision (of the customers you flag, how many really churn) and recall (of the real churners, how many you catch). With 3% positives, that is the trade-off that decides how many retention offers get wasted.
- **PR-AUC needs a baseline.** A random model scores about 0.03, which is your churn rate. So a PR-AUC of 0.25 means roughly 8 times better than random. Always say this baseline when you report it.

**How to present it to your manager:**
1. Lead with something like: "At the top 10% of customers we rank as most likely to churn, we catch X% of churners, and Y% of those we flag really do churn."
2. Give PR-AUC, with the 3% baseline, as the overall summary.
3. Include ROC-AUC only as a secondary number. It's fine to show, but it can make the model look better than it will perform in practice.

Whichever number you choose, report it on a held-out test set. If the data is time-ordered, split by time.
